summary: Explains how to produce DNSKEY and RRSIG records for DNSSEC using RSA with SHA-256 and SHA-512. These algorithms give DNSSEC stronger hash functions than SHA-1. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS answers can carry a digital signature that proves they are genuine. This document explains how to make that signature with RSA keys and the newer SHA-2 hash functions, which are considered harder to break than SHA-1.

questions: how to use sha-256 with rsa in dnssec
what key sizes does dnssec rsa sha-2 allow
why use sha-2 instead of sha-1 in dnssec
subtitle: How DNSSEC keys and signatures are made with RSA and the SHA-256 and SHA-512 hash functions.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC signatures used RSA with SHA-1, and confidence in SHA-1 was being eroded by recently announced attacks on that hash function.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds two algorithm numbers to the DNSSEC registry, 8 for RSA/SHA-256 and 10 for RSA/SHA-512, and states how the DNSKEY data is stored and how the RRSIG signature is computed.
tldr.outcome: Users of DNSSEC are encouraged to deploy SHA-2 as soon as software allows. The document is a Proposed Standard from October 2009 and is updated by RFC 6944.

facts.label: Key tag in the SHA-256 example

today: RFC 5702 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009. It is updated by RFC 6944 and has not been obsoleted, so the two algorithm numbers it registered remain part of the DNSSEC registry.

sections.title: Adding SHA-2 to DNSSEC
sections.content:
The Domain Name System is the global, hierarchical, distributed database for internet naming. DNSSEC extends it with cryptographic keys and digital signatures so that the authenticity and integrity of DNS data can be verified. RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 describe those security extensions, and RFC 4034 in particular stores DNSKEY and RRSIG resource records and lists the cryptographic algorithms to use.

RFC 5702 extends that list with RSA/SHA-256 and RSA/SHA-512. It states how to store the DNSKEY data and how to produce RRSIG resource records with these hash algorithms, and it assumes the reader already knows DNSSEC, RSA and the SHA-2 family. The name SHA-2 is used here only for SHA-256 and SHA-512, since SHA-224 and SHA-384 are not used in DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS has a list of ways to sign its answers. This document adds two stronger ways to that list, and says exactly how to build them.

sections.title: DNSKEY Records and Key Sizes
sections.content:
The format of the DNSKEY resource record is the one given in RFC 4034, and RFC 3110 describes the earlier use of RSA with SHA-1 for DNSSEC signatures.

RSA public keys for use with RSA/SHA-256 are stored in DNSKEY resource records with algorithm number 8. For interoperability, as in RFC 3110, the key size of RSA/SHA-256 keys MUST NOT be less than 512 bits and MUST NOT be more than 4096 bits. RSA public keys for use with RSA/SHA-512 are stored in DNSKEY resource records with algorithm number 10, and the key size of RSA/SHA-512 keys MUST NOT be less than 1024 bits and MUST NOT be more than 4096 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of signing gets a number badge, 8 or 10. Key sizes are limited, like locks that cannot be too tiny or too huge.

sections.title: Building the RRSIG Signature
sections.content:
The value of the signature field in the RRSIG resource record follows the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature scheme. First a hash is computed over the wire format data of the resource record set being signed, with hash = SHA-XXX(data), where XXX is either 256 or 512 depending on the algorithm used and as specified in FIPS PUB 180-3.

The signature is then computed as ( 00 | 01 | FF* | 00 | prefix | hash ) ** e (mod n), where the vertical bar is concatenation, the octets 00, 01, FF and 00 are fixed values, e is the private exponent of the signing RSA key and n is the public modulus of that key. The FF octet MUST be repeated the exact number of times so that the total length of the term in parentheses equals the length of the modulus.

The prefix exists so that standard cryptographic libraries can be used. The prefixes are taken from the RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 specifications in PKCS #1 v2.1 (Sections 8.2 and 9.2 of RFC 3447). RSA/SHA-256 signatures use algorithm number 8 with the ASN.1 DER SHA-256 algorithm designator prefix 30 31 30 0d 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 01 05 00 04 20. RSA/SHA-512 signatures use algorithm number 10 with the SHA-512 prefix 30 51 30 0d 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 03 05 00 04 40.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign, the software first squashes the record set into a short fingerprint. It then wraps that fingerprint in a standard envelope and locks the envelope with the private key.

sections.title: Key Sizes and Signature Sizes
sections.content:
Apart from the restrictions on key size in Section 2, the document does not say which size of key to use. It treats that as an operational issue that depends largely on the environment and the intended use, and points to NIST SP 800-57 as a good starting point for more information.

Signature size follows a simple rule in this family of algorithms: it depends on the size of the key and not on the hash algorithm used in the signing process. RRSIG resource records produced with RSA/SHA-256 or RSA/SHA-512 therefore have the same size as those produced with RSA/SHA-1 when the keys have the same length.
sections.plainLanguage: The document leaves the key length to the operator. One thing is certain: a stronger hash does not make the signature bigger.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Support
sections.content:
DNSSEC-aware implementations SHOULD be able to support RRSIG and DNSKEY resource records created with the RSA/SHA-2 algorithms defined here.

RFC 5155 defines new algorithm identifiers for existing signing algorithms so that zones signed with them can use NSEC3 as well as NSEC records to prove denial of existence. That mechanism was chosen to protect implementations that predate RFC 5155 from meeting resource records they could not know about. This document does not define such algorithm aliases. A DNSSEC validator that implements RSA/SHA-2 MUST be able to validate negative answers in the form of both NSEC and NSEC3 with hash algorithm 1 as defined in RFC 5155. An authoritative server that does not implement NSEC3 MAY still serve zones that use RSA/SHA-2 with NSEC denial of existence.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who checks signatures should be able to check both of the ways DNS says a name does not exist. A server that only knows one of them can still sign with the new algorithms.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The document gives a complete key and a complete signature for each algorithm, so that implementers can check their own software. In both examples the record set being signed is a single A record, www.example.net. 3600 IN A 192.0.2.91, the inception date is set at 00:00 hours on January 1st, 2000 and the expiration date at 00:00 hours on January 1st, 2030.

The RSA/SHA-256 example uses algorithm 8 and key tag 9033 with a 512-bit key, and the RSA/SHA-512 example uses algorithm 10 and key tag 3740 with a 1024-bit key. Each example lists the private key values in Base64, the resulting DNSKEY record and the RRSIG record that the key produces.
sections.plainLanguage: The document shows two finished examples so you can check that your own signing software produces the same result.

sections.title: IANA Registry Entries
sections.content: The document updates the IANA registry "DNS SECURITY ALGORITHM NUMBERS -- per RFC 4035" by adding two entries. Value 8 is RSA/SHA-256 with the mnemonic RSASHA256, and value 10 is RSA/SHA-512 with the mnemonic RSASHA512. Both are marked for zone signing. For both entries there has been no determination of standardization of the use of the algorithm with transaction security.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of DNSSEC algorithm numbers now has two new lines, 8 and 10, one for each new kind of signature.

sections.title: Why SHA-2 and Downgrade Resistance
sections.content:
Users of DNSSEC are encouraged to deploy SHA-2 as soon as software implementations allow for it. SHA-2 is widely believed to be more resilient to attack than SHA-1, and confidence in SHA-1's strength is being eroded by recently announced attacks. Whether or not those attacks affect DNSSEC, the document believed at the time of writing that SHA-2 is the better choice for DNSSEC records, and it considers SHA-2 sufficiently strong for the immediate future, while leaving predictions about the future of cryptography and cryptanalysis out of scope. The RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 scheme was chosen to match the one used for RSA/SHA-1, which should ease implementation of the new hash algorithms in DNSSEC software.

Downgrade attacks are handled by the signing rules themselves. Since each RRset MUST be signed with each algorithm present in the DNSKEY RRset at the zone apex (see Section 2.2 of RFC 4035), a malicious party cannot filter out the RSA/SHA-2 RRSIG and force the validator to use the RSA/SHA-1 signature when both are present in the zone. This gives resilience against algorithm downgrade attacks, provided the validator supports RSA/SHA-2.
sections.plainLanguage: If a zone publishes both an old and a new signature, an attacker cannot hide the new one to trick a checker into trusting only the older, weaker one.

viz.caption: HOW THE SIGNATURE IS COMPUTED (RFC 5702, SECTION 3)

data.title: RSA/SHA-2 signature computation
data.code:
hash = SHA-XXX(data)

signature = ( 00 | 01 | FF* | 00 | prefix | hash ) ** e (mod n)

00, 01, FF, 00 : fixed octets
prefix          : ASN.1 DER hash algorithm designator
e               : private exponent of the signing key
n               : public modulus of the signing key
